plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000063) on Central Park: Olmsted and Vaux's 1858 Greensward Plan, the designed landscape, sunken transverse roads, and the taking of Seneca Village by eminent domain. Topic checked against every bank and the combined bank (no matches). Ten new items with three NO CHANGE keys. Plus E062-08 and E062-09 (revision 2) and E062-10 (revision 3) resubmitted on banked passages CLD-P-ACT-E-000062 and 000061. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A Designed Wilderness
Oil on the Move
passages.text:
[1] Elijah McCoy was born in 1844 in Ontario, Canada, to parents who had escaped slavery in {{1|Kentucky, as a teenager, he}} traveled to Scotland to train as a mechanical engineer. [2] When he settled in Michigan, however, the only job he could find was as a fireman and oiler for the Michigan Central Railroad, {{2|shoveling coal and oiling the engine's moving parts}}.

[3] At the time, every train {{3|have}} to stop regularly so that workers could oil its engine by hand. [4] In 1872, McCoy patented an automatic lubricator, a cup that dripped oil {{4|steadily and continuously at a constant rate}} into an engine while it ran. [5] Railroads that adopted the device saved time and money, {{5|since}} engines no longer had to stop for oiling.

[6] McCoy {{9|went on to receive}} more than fifty patents, including ones for a folding ironing board and a lawn sprinkler. [7] Some historians believe that the expression "the real McCoy" came from engineers who insisted on {{6|McCoys'}} lubricator rather than imitations, though the phrase's origin is disputed. [8] {{7|For example,}} McCoy's {{8|inventions, kept}} trains and factory machines running more smoothly for decades.

passages.title: Every Man Home
passages.text:
[1] In August 1914, Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance left England for Antarctica, where he hoped to lead the first crossing of the continent on foot. [2] In January 1915, the pack ice of the Weddell Sea closed around the {{1|ship, the crew}} could do nothing but wait. [3] For months the ice slowly squeezed the hull, and in November 1915 Endurance {{2|sunk}} beneath it.

[4] The twenty-eight men camped on the drifting ice for months. [5] When the ice began to break up in April 1916, they {{3|rowed three lifeboats to Elephant Island, a barren, uninhabited place}}. [6] Knowing that no ship would search such a remote spot, Shackleton and five companions sailed one lifeboat about 800 miles across stormy seas to South Georgia, {{4|which}} a whaling station operated.

[7] Because they had landed on the island's empty side, Shackleton and two others then {{5|hiked and walked}} across its unmapped mountains to reach the station. [8] It took four attempts, but in August 1916 Shackleton {{6|finally}} reached Elephant Island and rescued all twenty-two men waiting there. [9] Not one member of the crew {{7|were lost}}.

[10] In 2022, an expedition found the wreck of Endurance nearly 10,000 feet below the surface of the Weddell {{8|Sea; remarkably well}} preserved.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: plan, which they called the Greensward Plan
candidates.explanation: "Their plan ... imagined meadows" is an independent clause, so a period correctly separates it from the first sentence.

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from its clause.

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Separate independent clauses with a period or semicolon.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: a lot of very many trees
choices.C: trees, many thousands of them, numerous
choices.D: many thousands of trees in large numbers

candidates.evidence: Workers blasted rock, moved earth, and planted
candidates.explanation: "Many thousands of trees" states the amount once, clearly and concisely.

B.rationale: "A lot of very many" is wordy and redundant.

C.rationale: "Many thousands" and "numerous" repeat the same idea.

hints: Which choice says the idea once?

strategy.explanation: Choose the most concise clear option.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: almost every hill and pond was designed
candidates.explanation: The park looks natural, yet it was designed, so the concessive "Although" fits.

B.rationale: The park's natural look is not the reason it was designed.

C.rationale: "Since" signals a cause, but the two clauses contrast.

D.rationale: "Unless" makes the design conditional, which does not make sense.

hints: Do the two clauses agree or contrast?
candidates.remember: Use "although" when one clause concedes a point the other contradicts.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.A: also tucked roads below for crosstown traffic
choices.B: tucked also roads for crosstown traffic
choices.C: also tucked, for crosstown traffic, roads
choices.D: also tucked roads for crosstown traffic

candidates.evidence: below the level of the park
candidates.explanation: "Also tucked roads for crosstown traffic below the level of the park" keeps each modifier next to the words it modifies.

A.rationale: "Below" is now separated from "the level of the park" and the sentence becomes confusing.

B.rationale: Placing "also" between the verb and its object is awkward and unidiomatic.

C.rationale: Setting off "for crosstown traffic" separates the verb from its object awkwardly.

strategy.explanation: Read each option in the full sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep modifiers next to the words they describe.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
These sunken roads, called transverse roads, still carry traffic across the park today.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: No, because it shifts the focus from the park's design to modern traffic laws.
choices.B: No, because it repeats information already given in sentence 5.
choices.C: Yes, because it adds a relevant detail about the roads just described.
choices.D: Yes, because it explains why Olmsted and Vaux won the design competition.

candidates.evidence: so that carriages could cross it without disturbing visitors
candidates.explanation: The added sentence names the roads just described and notes their continued use, which supports the paragraph's point about the park's design.

A.rationale: The sentence is about the roads' continued use, not traffic laws.

B.rationale: Sentence 5 does not name the roads or say they are still used.

D.rationale: The sentence says nothing about the competition.

hints: Is the sentence connected to sentence 5?

strategy.explanation: Compare the sentence with the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence if it supports the paragraph's point.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: a community of mostly African American
candidates.explanation: The community was made up of many homeowners, so the plural "homeowners" with no apostrophe is correct.

A.rationale: "Homeowner's" is singular possessive, but the sentence needs a plural noun.

B.rationale: "Homeowners'" is a plural possessive, but nothing follows that they possess.

C.rationale: "Homeowner" is singular, but a community has many homeowners.

hints: Does anything belong to the homeowners here?

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The series "churches, homes, and school" is the subject; no comma should come between it and the verb "were."

A.rationale: A comma should not separate the compound subject from its verb "were."

D.rationale: The commas are misplaced, and one separates the subject from the verb.

strategy.explanation: Read the subject and verb together.

candidates.remember: Do not put a comma between a subject and its verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Today" calls for the present tense, so "draws" is correct.

B.rationale: The past tense does not fit "Today."

C.rationale: The past perfect does not fit "Today."

D.rationale: The future perfect does not fit "Today."

strategy.explanation: Match the verb to the time marker.

candidates.remember: Use the present tense for current facts.

candidates.subskill: Concluding sentence (connecting to the previous paragraph)
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by connecting the park's present to the cost described in the third paragraph?

choices.B: The park includes a zoo, several ponds, and an ice rink.
choices.C: Olmsted went on to design parks in many other American cities.
choices.D: Central Park covers more than 800 acres in the middle of Manhattan.

candidates.evidence: including the residents of Seneca Village
candidates.explanation: The question asks for a conclusion that connects the present park to the cost of its creation; only the current sentence mentions remembering Seneca Village.

B.rationale: This lists features but does not connect to the cost described earlier.

C.rationale: This shifts to Olmsted's later career.

D.rationale: This gives the park's size, not a connection to its cost.

hints: What cost does the third paragraph describe?

strategy.explanation: Match each choice to the stated goal.

candidates.remember: Choose the conclusion that meets the specific goal.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how Central Park was designed to look natural. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it describes in detail how every tree in the park was chosen.
choices.B: No, because it treats the design briefly and turns to the park's human cost.
choices.C: Yes, because its main focus is the engineering of the transverse roads.
choices.D: No, because it never says that the park was designed rather than natural.

candidates.evidence: almost every hill and pond was designed
candidates.explanation: The essay mentions the designed landscape briefly but devotes much of its length to the displacement of Seneca Village, so it does not mainly explain the natural-looking design.

A.rationale: The essay does not describe how trees were chosen.

C.rationale: The roads are mentioned in one sentence.

D.rationale: Sentence 4 says almost every hill and pond was designed.

hints: How much of the essay is about the design?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the exact purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Remarkably well preserved" describes the wreck and is correctly set off by a comma.

A.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "remarkably well preserved" is not one.

B.rationale: Without a comma, the phrase seems to describe the sea.

C.rationale: "And" joins nothing parallel; the phrase is not a second item or clause.

strategy.explanation: Check what each punctuation mark requires.

candidates.remember: Use a comma to set off a descriptive phrase at the end of a sentence.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: colon choice arguably defensible before an elaborating phrase
revision_history.change: colon choice replaced with a clearly ungrammatical conjunction

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe a scientific discovery made during an Antarctic expedition. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains how the pack ice of the Weddell Sea forms.
choices.B: Yes, because it reports that the wreck was found in 2022.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the crew's survival and rescue.
choices.D: No, because it never mentions Antarctica or the Weddell Sea.

candidates.evidence: rescued all twenty-two men waiting there
candidates.explanation: The essay tells how the crew survived and were rescued; it describes no scientific discovery made during the expedition.

A.rationale: The essay does not explain how pack ice forms.

B.rationale: Finding the wreck is a search result, not a discovery made during the expedition.

hints: What is the essay mostly about?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against the exact purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: key wording "not a scientific discovery" too absolute
revision_history.change: key reworded to "focuses mainly on the crew's survival"

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: steadily and at a steady pace

candidates.explanation: "Steadily" expresses the idea once, without repetition.

A.rationale: "Steadily," "continuously," and "at a constant rate" all say the same thing.

B.rationale: "Steadily" and "at a steady pace" say the same thing.

D.rationale: "Continuously" and "without ever stopping" mean the same thing.

hints: Do any words repeat the same idea?

strategy.explanation: Choose the most concise option that keeps the meaning.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: B ("steadily and continuously") only mildly redundant and arguably defensible
revision_history.change: B replaced with a plainly redundant pair

revision_history.reason: both solvers: D ("continuously at a constant rate") not strictly redundant
revision_history.change: D replaced with a true doublet
